body:
Which IE version did you use ? Should be a recent one on Windows 8, but keep in mind that the JQuery version used by the GUI (v2) isn't compatible with older IE versions.
I tried with IE 11 and the Ajax request are made without problem and return the right JSON or text values.

But some commit broke the discovery on Windows, I now get the error : "discover: 16:41:56.946712 discover.go:84: setsockopt: The requested address is not valid in its context.; not joining on {7FBB46E0-5892-4942-9410-492F2FE1A542}"

That's a debug error... But yeah, modern enough Windows I think. Something is either really broken with my Windows install or with Syncthing under Windows, and I'm kind of leaning towards the latter since you are probably the only one having done any reasonable amount of testing. :) I'll get to it at some point, because I'd like it to work.

I'm pretty sure that it worked before the IPv6 commit. I'll have a closer look whenever I find some time, but I already found something weird. The `net.Interfaces()` shows IPv4 addresses but after the `disc.conn.JoinGroup()` it sends discovery announces with only the IPv6 addresses linked to that interface and not the IPv4 ones, which is really weird. On Linux the `net.Interfaces()` returns all the IPs linked to all interfaces, which is not the same behaviour as on Windows. For the error in my previous post, it was because I disabled IPv6 on my Windows 8, which broke basically the whole discovery (maybe there should be an IPv4-only alternative?).

For the GUI, the AngularJS doc says that there should be an `id="ng-app"` on the `<html>` tag for IE support (see http://docs.angularjs.org/guide/ie).

I'll open an issue when I find some more information.

Hmm, yeah, I kinda assumed no systems were without IPv6 support nowadays. At least on the Mac and Linux side of things it's on by default and mostly essential. I could still have broken something on Windows though, it was when I tested for that that I discovered mostly nothing worked as expected and got disheartened. :) :(

For the GUI, could be as easy as the angular stuff being done wrong, yeah.

Another point is the terminal windows. Making so that it doesn't show up is easy enough, but that leaves the user without a way to shut down. Would not showing the terminal window and adding a shutdown option to the gui make sense?
In other words; barring the effort of making an actual Windows GUI, how do we make it suck as little as possible? :)

IPv6 is enabled on Windows 7 and above by default I think, maybe Windows Vista too, I just disabled it.
I think it would make sense to have an option in the GUI, but how could you be sure that the user knows the URL to access the GUI ? Maybe some kind of tray icon could be useful, although I don't know how to make one in Go.

In general, having everything (including the logs) in the GUI would be nice, even for linux where the service could then run without needing some virtual terminal or things like that.

But getting the syncing to work on Windows would already be nice, even without GUI.

Yeah, probably you can't. The thing that would need to be done (same for Mac, really) would be to have a wrapper written in something native that just starts/stops the "real" syncthing binary, shows it's status and opens the HTTP GUI when clicked, or something like that. I.e. a tray icon on Windows, a menubar thingy on Mac (#42).
Yes, there probably should be something like that, and it may even be easy to do (https://gowalker.org/github.com/cratonica/trayhost).
Well, just saw that this library can't be cross-compiled :(
I guessed as much. If and when this gets relevant I think doing native builds per OS will be reasonable.

Well, actually it's easier than that. The problem is that I get a `HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified` on every ajax request made, so the values are always the same. Maybe there's some caching involved? But there is no `If-Modified-Since` in the request headers, strange.

Guess adding `Cache-Control: no-cache` to every request would do it.
